prompt: Let $f(x) = x^2 + a$ for $x < 1$, $f(1) = 5$, and $f(x) = bx + 2$ for $x > 1$. If $f$ is continuous at $x = 1$, what is $a + b$?
hint: Continuity at $1$ means BOTH one-sided limits must equal $f(1) = 5$. That gives you two separate equations.

hints.text: Continuity at $1$ means BOTH one-sided limits must equal $f(1) = 5$. That gives you two separate equations.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Warm up: if $f(x) = x + a$ for $x < 1$ and $f(1) = 5$, the left limit $1 + a$ must be $5$, so $a = 4$. Now do the same for each side of this problem.

explanation: Left-hand limit: $\lim_{x \to 1^-} (x^2 + a) = 1 + a$. Set equal to $f(1) = 5$: $a = 4$.
Right-hand limit: $\lim_{x \to 1^+} (bx + 2) = b + 2$. Set equal to $5$: $b = 3$.

alternativeExplanations.title: Verify the stitched graph
steps: With $a = 4$: the parabola $x^2 + 4$ arrives at height $5$ as $x \to 1$.
With $b = 3$: the line $3x + 2$ leaves from height $5$ as $x \to 1$.
The dot $f(1) = 5$ sits exactly where both pieces meet — three conditions, all satisfied.
